title: Simpson's Paradox
objective: After this level you can explain how a trend in every group can reverse when the groups are combined, using the 1973 Berkeley admissions data.
summary: Berkeley admitted 44% of men and 35% of women in 1973, yet women did better in four of the six biggest departments. A trend in every group can reverse when the groups are combined.

cards.headline: In 1973, Berkeley seemed to favor men. Department by department, it didn't.
cards.body: The overall numbers looked damning. Then researchers looked one department at a time, and the pattern turned around. Same applicants, same decisions, opposite story. How can both be true?

cards.headline: The overall numbers
cards.body: In fall 1973, Berkeley's graduate programs admitted about 44% of the 8,442 men who applied, but only about 35% of the 4,321 women. That's a gap of 9 percentage points. Level 2 showed that percents put groups of different sizes on one scale, so this looks like a fair comparison. Hold that thought.

cards.headline: Inside the departments
cards.body: Split the numbers by department and they flip. In Department A, one of the six biggest, 82% of the 108 women who applied got in, against 62% of the 825 men. In four of those six departments, women were admitted at a higher rate. The difference was where people applied: women more often chose departments that were hard to get into, men the easier ones.

cards.fact: A trend in every group can reverse when the groups are combined.
cards.context: That's Simpson's paradox. Berkeley's overall percents mixed departments with very different odds, so they partly measured who applied where. In a 1975 paper in Science, three researchers found a small bias in favor of women once departments were taken into account. Before trusting a combined percent, ask what it lumps together.

cards.headline: Simpson's paradox: spotted
learned: Berkeley 1973: 44% of men, 35% of women admitted
Department A: 82% of women, 62% of men
Women applied more to hard departments
A combined percent can hide the groups' story

questions.explanation: Simpson's paradox: a trend that holds in each group disappears or reverses once the groups are pooled, as at Berkeley in 1973.

questions.prompt: Hospital A has better survival than Hospital B for mild cases and for severe cases, but worse survival overall. What's the likeliest explanation?

options.label: Someone made a mistake, since that's impossible
options.rationale: It's entirely possible; that's Simpson's paradox.

options.label: Hospital B treats more patients in total
options.rationale: Size alone doesn't flip a trend; the mix of cases does.

options.label: Hospital A's care is worse overall
options.rationale: It does better with both kinds of case.

options.label: Hospital A treats a far bigger share of severe cases

questions.explanation: Like women applying to hard departments at Berkeley, Hospital A takes on more of the hardest cases, which drags down its combined rate.

questions.prompt: Level 2 says percents let you compare groups of different sizes. Why did Berkeley's overall percents still mislead?

options.label: The groups were too different in size for percents
options.rationale: Percents handle different sizes; the problem was the mix of departments.

options.label: They lumped together departments with very different odds
Percents only work out of exactly 100 people
options.rationale: Percents work for any group size; that's their point.

options.label: The men's percent was calculated wrongly
options.rationale: The arithmetic was right; the combining misled.

questions.explanation: Each percent was correct, but pooling hard and easy departments made the totals reflect who applied where.
